difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: one concept (the cuboid count of a data cube with concept hierarchies) needing direct recall of the formula and a single-step computation, (3+1)^3 = 64; about 1 minute.
stem:
Consider the concept hierarchies as shown in the figure.

Which of the following options denotes the total number of possible data cuboids from these concept hierarchies?

![Figure: Three concept hierarchies drawn as vertical chains of three levels each. First: Year at the top, then Month, then Day. Second: Country at the top, then State, then City. Third: Item Category at the top, then Item Type, then Item.](/pyq/2026/fig/Q43-1.png)

solution.quick:
There are 3 dimensions (time, location, item), each with $L_i = 3$ hierarchy levels. A cuboid chooses, for each dimension, one of its levels or the virtual top level "all", so each dimension offers $L_i + 1 = 4$ choices.

Total cuboids $= \prod_i (L_i + 1) = 4 \times 4 \times 4 = 4^3 = 64$. **(A)**

steps.title: Read the dimensions and their levels
steps.body:
The figure shows three dimensions, each with a 3-level concept hierarchy (lowest level at the bottom):

| Dimension | Levels (fine → coarse) | $L_i$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| time | Day → Month → Year | 3 |
| location | City → State → Country | 3 |
| item | Item → Item Type → Item Category | 3 |

steps.title: Formula: cuboids of a cube with hierarchies
steps.body:
A cuboid is fixed by deciding, independently for each dimension, the level at which that dimension is summarised. Each dimension can sit at any of its $L_i$ levels, **or** be aggregated away completely, which corresponds to the virtual top level $\text{all}$. That gives $L_i + 1$ choices per dimension, and the choices multiply:

$$
T = \prod_{i=1}^{n} (L_i + 1)
$$

steps.title: Substitute and compute
steps.body:
With $n = 3$ and $L_1 = L_2 = L_3 = 3$:

$$
T = (3 + 1)(3 + 1)(3 + 1) = 4^3 = 64
$$

Examples: $(\text{Day}, \text{City}, \text{Item})$ is the base cuboid, $(\text{Month}, \text{Country}, \text{all})$ is an intermediate cuboid, and $(\text{all}, \text{all}, \text{all})$ is the apex cuboid (the grand total).

steps.title: Sanity check and answer
steps.body:
Without hierarchies ($L_i = 1$ for each dimension) the formula gives $2^3 = 8$, the familiar count of all subsets of 3 dimensions. The hierarchies enlarge this lattice to $4^3 = 64$ cuboids.

Answer → **(A)** $4^3$.

solution.teaching:
**Data cube and cuboids.** In a data warehouse, a fact such as sales is analysed along dimensions such as time, location and item. A *cuboid* is one summary table of the facts at a particular granularity, for example "total sales per Month per Country". The set of all cuboids forms a lattice called the **data cube**. At the bottom is the **base cuboid**, the finest granularity in every dimension. At the top is the **apex cuboid**, where every dimension is aggregated away and a single grand total remains.

**Without hierarchies.** If each dimension has just one level, a cuboid is decided by which dimensions it keeps. Each dimension is either kept or dropped, so $n$ dimensions give $2^n$ cuboids.

**With concept hierarchies.** A concept hierarchy orders a dimension's levels from fine to coarse, such as $\text{Day} \prec \text{Month} \prec \text{Year}$. Rolling up moves up the hierarchy, and drilling down moves back down. Now a cuboid decides, for every dimension, *which level* to use, or to drop the dimension entirely, which is the extra virtual top level $\text{all}$. So a dimension with $L_i$ levels contributes $L_i + 1$ choices, and because the dimensions are chosen independently the counts multiply:

$$
T = \prod_{i=1}^{n} (L_i + 1).
$$

(This is the standard result stated in Han, Kamber and Pei's *Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques*.)

**Applying it here.** Each of the three hierarchies (Year–Month–Day, Country–State–City, Item Category–Item Type–Item) has 3 levels, so each dimension has $3 + 1 = 4$ choices. The total is $4 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 = 4^3 = 64$. Remember the "+1": forgetting the $\text{all}$ level gives $3^3 = 27$, and ignoring the hierarchies gives $2^3 = 8$.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Each of the 3 dimensions has 3 levels plus the virtual level $\text{all}$, so 4 choices per dimension and $4 \times 4 \times 4 = 4^3 = 64$ cuboids.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $2^3 = 8$ counts cuboids only when each dimension has a single level (keep it or drop it). It ignores the 3-level concept hierarchies shown in the figure.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $2! = 2$ is far too small: the base cuboid $(\text{Day}, \text{City}, \text{Item})$ and the apex cuboid $(\text{all}, \text{all}, \text{all})$ are already 2 cuboids, and $(\text{Year}, \text{all}, \text{all})$ is a third.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $4! = 24$ counts orderings, but a cuboid is a combination of independent level choices, one per dimension. The choices multiply as $4 \times 4 \times 4$, not $4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1$.

solution.shortcut: For each dimension take (number of hierarchy levels $+ 1$) and multiply across dimensions. Here that is $(3+1)^3 = 4^3$.
solution.commonTrap: Using the plain $2^n$ lattice count ($2^3 = 8$, option B), which ignores the hierarchies, or forgetting the "+1" for the virtual top level $\text{all}$ and getting $3^3 = 27$.

answerVerification.method: Author solve (not blind) compared with official key
answerVerification.checkCode:
from itertools import product
levels={'time':['Day','Month','Year'],'location':['City','State','Country'],'item':['Item','Item Type','Item Category']}
choices=[lv+['all'] for lv in levels.values()]   # each dimension: one of its 3 levels, or rolled up to 'all'
cuboids=list(product(*choices)); print(len(cuboids), 4**3, 2**3); assert len(cuboids)==4**3==64
answerVerification.notes: Three dimensions with 3-level hierarchies each (Year–Month–Day, Country–State–City, Item Category–Item Type–Item). The cuboid count is the product of (L_i + 1) over dimensions = 4^3 = 64; enumeration in Python confirms 64. This matches official key A.
